## When the Base Moves, Every Shortcut Changes {#sec-lay-ch17}

## A Concrete Picture

Swing a pendulum while standing on a rolling board. Your hand accelerates the
pendulum, and its reaction can move you and the board. Now imagine a powerful
actuator holding your hand to a recorded trajectory. The hand can still move,
but the pendulum cannot change its assigned path. The actuator supplies the
reaction needed to maintain that motion.

These experiments answer different questions. A prescribed hand path lets us
calculate a club response or infer loads compatible with measured motion. A
finite-mass base lets the body-side motion respond to the loading. Comparing
them is useful only when we say which inputs change, which motions are enforced,
and where the enforcing force and its work enter the calculation.

![Both Bases Can Move: One Follows an Assigned Trajectory, While the Other Responds to Force and Inertia.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_prescribed_vs_moving_base.svg){#fig-lay-moving-base width=97% fig-alt="Two vertically arranged schematics show a translating base connected to arm and club links. The prescribed case requires a reported enforcing reaction and power; the finite-mass case lets club loading change the base motion. Arrows are qualitative, not measured force vectors."}

## How the Mechanism Works

### The Boundary Condition Comes First

A **fixed base** is constrained to remain stationary. A **prescribed base** has
a specified position and orientation as functions of time; stationary support is
one special case. A **dynamic base** has equations of motion in which applied
loads, inertia, gravity, contacts, and constraints determine its acceleration.
None of these descriptions alone identifies a golfer's muscles or controller.

For prescribed motion, the enforcing reaction is the residual needed after the
other loads have been declared. It may be large even when the trajectory looks
smooth. Multiple contacts can leave the allocation of that reaction nonunique.
Calling the trajectory measured improves its connection to an observed trial;
it does not make the motion responsive to a new control strategy.

Assigning an applied force as well as a prescribed trajectory is not automatically
an error. It is a well-defined experiment if an additional constraint reaction
absorbs the difference and its work is reported. The error is to treat the
assigned force as the sole cause of the motion while silently allowing the
trajectory actuator to supply the remaining force and energy.

#### Finite Mass Is Not a Trajectory Actuator

A translating body's acceleration decreases as its mass increases under a
bounded resultant force. In a simple translating-base limit with a fixed time
interval and initial velocity, increasing
mass does not produce an arbitrary accelerating hand path. Maintaining such a
path instead requires an appropriately increasing force. Mass, stiffness,
feedback gain, and actuator force capacity are different model assumptions.

A reduced moving hub also remains a reduced hub. Adding finite mass does not
supply pelvis and trunk dynamics, shoulder anatomy, balance, or realistic ground
contact. Its value is that one formerly imposed motion can now respond to load.

### A Small Model That Makes the Difference Visible

Consider a cart of mass $M$ on a frictionless horizontal track. A point bob of mass
$m$ is attached by a massless rigid link of length $l$. Let $x$ be cart position
and $\theta$ the link angle from downward vertical, so the bob is at
$(x+l\sin\theta,-l\cos\theta)$. Apply horizontal cart force $F$ and pivot torque
$\tau$, positive with increasing $\theta$. The cart does not rotate; the support
moment that maintains this orientation has zero angular power.
Take $M,m,l>0$ and let $g$ be the magnitude of gravitational acceleration.

In an inertial frame, the equations are

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
M+m & ml\cos\theta\\
ml\cos\theta & ml^2
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\ddot x\\\ddot\theta\end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix}
-ml\sin\theta\,\dot\theta^2\\
mgl\sin\theta
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}F\\\tau\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The first row is total horizontal momentum balance. The second is the bob's
tangential balance about its moving pivot. Both rows are needed: the pivot
acceleration is part of the bob's equation, while the bob contributes to the
force needed to accelerate the cart.

Use the **manufactured** values $M=2\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m=1\,\mathrm{kg}$,
$l=1\,\mathrm m$, and $\theta=\dot\theta=0$. Keep $\tau=1\,\mathrm{N\,m}$.
The following are simultaneous accelerations at that state, not measured golf
results or finite-duration performance predictions. Force entries are in newtons;
the acceleration pair is $(\ddot x,\ddot\theta)$ in
$\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-2}}$, respectively.

| Experiment | Applied $F$ | Extra Enforcing Force $\lambda$ | Acceleration Pair |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Free cart, baseline | 3 | 0 | $(1,0)$ |
| Free cart, remove $F$ | 0 | 0 | $(-0.5,1.5)$ |
| Enforce baseline cart acceleration after removing $F$ | 0 | 3 | $(1,0)$ |

The free-cart intervention changes both accelerations. The prescribed replay
instead replaces the removed force with $\lambda$. Its unchanged pendulum
response does not show that the original cart force was unimportant. It shows
that another driver is now enforcing the same base motion.

#### Coordinate Changes Do Not Remove Physical Coupling

Off-diagonal inertia terms are informative in a declared coordinate system, but
they are not a coordinate-independent definition of mechanical interaction.
For this example, put $a=ml/(M+m)$ and use the horizontal center-of-mass coordinate
$r=x+a\sin\theta$. The kinetic energy becomes diagonal:

$$
T=\frac12(M+m)\dot r^2+
\frac12\left(ml^2-\frac{m^2l^2}{M+m}\cos^2\theta\right)\dot\theta^2.
$$

However, the same applied loads have virtual work

$$
F\,\delta x+\tau\,\delta\theta
=F\,\delta r+(\tau-aF\cos\theta)\,\delta\theta.
$$

The cart force still contributes to the angular equation. A coordinate change
moves terms between the inertia description and the generalized loads; it does
not alter the physical accelerations. Convective terms, gravity, constraints,
and the way controls enter the equations must travel with the coordinate change.

### What a Counterfactual Can Establish

Start two free-base simulations from the same compatible state. Keep the distal
input history fixed and remove a declared base input from one branch. Compare
instantaneous accelerations before either trajectory has moved. Then integrate
them and compare the accumulated changes in base motion, contact loads, club
speed, and work. This identifies an effect of that intervention **within the
specified model**, not a physiological strategy effect by itself.

Now prescribe the baseline base trajectory. If the removed input enters only
the base equations, while distal equations, inputs, and initial state remain
identical, the baseline distal trajectory solves the replay problem too. Under
uniqueness it is the same solution; the enforcing reaction supplies the missing
base load. **Baseline replay is a consistency check, not evidence that dynamic
feedback was unimportant.** The acceleration table is an instantaneous example;
a trajectory comparison additionally needs compatible position and velocity.

This conclusion has limits. Removing an actuator that also supplies a distal
generalized load need not leave the distal equations unchanged. Discontinuous
contact changes, incompatible constraints, or a different initial state can also
invalidate the comparison. State those changes instead of attributing every
difference to feedback.

Keeping a torque **history** fixed differs from keeping a feedback **policy**
fixed. A policy evaluated along diverging trajectories can issue different
commands. Both experiments can be useful: the first isolates a prescribed input
comparison, while the second evaluates the chosen controller interacting with
the altered mechanics. They estimate different effects and should not share one
unqualified label such as “proximal contribution.”

### Follow Work Across the Same Boundary

For a declared collection of bodies in an inertial frame, a useful mechanical
ledger is

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\left(T+U_g+U_{\rm shaft}+U_{\rm contact}\right)
=P_{\rm act}+P_{\rm other,ext}-D,
\qquad D\ge0.
$$

Here $T$ includes the kinetic energy of every included body and any represented
flexible modes. The $U$ terms are the conservative gravitational, shaft, and
contact energies actually present in that model; absent elements contribute
nothing. $P_{\rm act}$ is the power of the declared actuators, including any
trajectory-enforcing actuator; $P_{\rm other,ext}$ is other external power not
already represented by the conservative potentials. Dissipation $D$ includes
the specified damping or friction losses.
Account for gravity through $U_g$ or through gravitational power, not both.
Likewise, shaft work entering stored energy is not an additional unexplained
whole-system energy input.

If the prescribed base coordinate is $x$, its enforcing actuator contributes
$\lambda\dot x$. For several prescribed coordinates the corresponding term is
$\boldsymbol\lambda^\top\dot{\mathbf q}_b$, where $\mathbf q_b$ contains the
prescribed coordinates and $\boldsymbol\lambda$ their power-conjugate enforcing
loads. In the cart example, $E=T+mgl(1-\cos\theta)$ and

$$
\dot E=(F+\lambda)\dot x+\tau\dot\theta.
$$

The force needed to enforce motion is not free merely because the solver calls
it a constraint reaction. At an instant with zero base velocity, that reaction
can change acceleration while doing zero instantaneous translational work.

When the system boundary includes both sides of an ideal passive internal joint, their
constraint powers cancel under its compatible relative motion. A compliant
interface instead exchanges energy with its storage and dissipative elements.
Do not add club-side contact power as a new external input to an enlarged system
that already contains the hand, club, and interface. Relative joint motion is
power-conjugate to an internal actuator torque; an absolute segment angular
velocity generally is not. These distinctions connect the moving-base question
to the ledgers in @sec-lay-ch05 and @sec-lay-ch10.

Numerical convergence tests whether the computed result stabilizes under a
specified refinement. It does not establish that the contact law, controller,
or anatomy is valid. Check force and moment balance, power signs, bookkeeping,
and constraint-projection work separately; report any residual with its scale
and refinement behavior rather than treating a small energy residual as a
universal validation certificate.

#### The Moving-Handle Contribution

For a rigid club, let $H$ be a handle point, $C$ a head point,
$\mathbf r_{C/H}$ the vector from $H$ to $C$, and $\boldsymbol\omega$ the club's
angular velocity. Their inertial-frame velocities satisfy
$\mathbf v_C=\mathbf v_H+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_{C/H}$.
A flexible club needs its additional deformation velocity under a declared
reference description. Changing handle motion can therefore change head speed,
club loading, and relative release together. An inward handle motion is not a
universal speed instruction: its effect depends on timing, force, orientation,
shaft state, and the rest of the trajectory.

For a locally rigid grip region, let $\mathbf F_H$ be the resultant force on
the club and $\mathbf M_H$ its moment about $H$. With grip velocity
$\mathbf v_H$ and angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega_H$, their power is

$$
P_H=\mathbf F_H\cdot\mathbf v_H+
\mathbf M_H\cdot\boldsymbol\omega_H.
$$

A negative projected moment is neither this total power nor its time integral.
Even negative rotational power can coexist with positive translational power.
Moving the wrench reduction point changes its moment and the separate power
terms; consistent transport preserves their total for the same rigid-body
loading and twist. It does not permit treating a flexible assembly as one rigid
body without accounting for deformation work.

## Where the Picture Breaks

### What the Provider Benchmarks Establish

The pinned coupled-base/flex study supplies a reduced planar example with
explicit base dynamics, grip and shaft moments, and a constrained solve. Its
registered driver-removal branch follows a short, 50 ms continuation from the
selected state. The spatial study instead uses finite-mass hand carriages,
compliant contact forces, and a rigid club. Its archived driver-removal traces
retain the provider-defined negative projected contact moment for a bounded
37.5 ms interval. These are model results with declared inputs and observables,
not estimates of a typical golfer's passive release duration.

MuJoCo and Pinocchio provide separate native inertia and bias operators in the
spatial comparison. The experiment shares its contact law and integration
procedure, so agreement is narrower than two independently developed physical
models reproducing a human experiment. A reproducible sign within that shared
construction can motivate a further test without establishing physiological
passivity, net energy transfer, or robustness over untested parameters.

#### Force Closure Is Not the Whole Contact Contract

The spatial force-pair limitation already discussed in @sec-lay-ch20 matters
here too. With club-point position $\mathbf p$, hand-point position $\mathbf h$, displacement
$\boldsymbol\delta=\mathbf h-\mathbf p$, and the supplied law
$\mathbf F=k\boldsymbol\delta+c\dot{\boldsymbol\delta}$, where $k$ is stiffness
and $c$ is damping coefficient, applying $+\mathbf F$ at the club point and
$-\mathbf F$ at the hand point gives zero resultant force but pair moment

$$
(\mathbf p-\mathbf h)\times\mathbf F
=-c\boldsymbol\delta\times\dot{\boldsymbol\delta}.
$$

The central spring contribution vanishes; the general vector damping
contribution need not. Calling this a closed internal interface requires the
corresponding connector moment or angular-momentum account, or an explicit
external torque pathway. The existing power identity and native-engine
agreement do not supply that missing interpretation. This qualification is not
proof that the pair moment causes the reported negative club moment. Changing
the contact law or adding a couple changes the dynamics and power ledger, so
one must rerun the registered trajectories before claiming the sign survives.
The central-fiber model discussed in @sec-lay-ch16 has a different contact law;
the diagnosis cannot be transferred to it by name alone.

#### Declare the Moment Point, Axis, and Geometry Control

The spatial record reduces its contact wrench at the club reference point. Its
signed projection uses a normalized cross product of the club longitudinal axis
and that point's linear velocity, with a declared world-axis fallback and sign
convention. This is a chosen observable, not a universal anatomical swing-plane
normal. Near a degenerate cross product, the fallback and sign convention need
to be exposed in the record.

Expressing the same physical moment and axis in another orthonormal frame
preserves their dot product. Changing the moment reference point, changing the
axis, or moving a contact point is a different operation. The spatial
coincident-point and reversed-arm controls recompute moments from the same
force traces; they test wrench geometry, not newly simulated contact
trajectories. The planar coincident-grip control does run a new continuation.
A one-arm benchmark also needs explicit second-hand contacts and controls before
it can answer a two-hand allocation question.

### Human Evidence and Strategy

Nesbit and McGinnis analyze one selected swing from each of four right-handed
amateurs. Their three-dimensional marker measurements are mapped into a rigid
planar club model to infer loads and examine hub-path effects. This supports a
mechanical reason to include handle motion; it is not a population intervention
showing that an imposed path improves performance [@nesbit2009hub].

Miura combines measured examples with simplified moving-pivot models to examine
inward pulling and parametric acceleration. A prescribed-pivot model explains
a possible route for work to enter the club under its assumptions. It does not
establish the required whole-body control, energy cost, or benefit for every
golfer [@miura2001]. The relation among measured motion, inferred loads, and
biological explanations is developed further in @sec-lay-ch24.

Testing a body-side strategy needs synchronized whole-body and club motion,
external and interface load estimates, inertial parameters, and uncertainty in
joint centers and soft-tissue motion. A force plate constrains an external
wrench; it does not identify individual muscle forces. A handle driver can be a
useful reduced input without acquiring anatomical precision from its name.

Declare the model, controller, comparison, and failure criterion before testing.
If their combination fails, that result counts against the tested combination.
Blaming the controller rather than the proposed mechanism requires additional
comparisons or evidence. A state-triggered command may transfer better across
base tempo than a clock-triggered one, but that remains a hypothesis to assess
on held-out conditions with observable triggers and appropriate load limits.

## Reader Lab: Prescribe, Then Release

Begin with the manufactured cart example. Verify the acceleration table from
both Newton balances and the coupled equations. Compare the energy rate with
applied and enforcing power. Then simulate a baseline, remove $F$ with the cart
free, and replay the baseline cart trajectory under the same distal torque.
Report which reaction replaces the removed force and the numerical tolerance
of the replay comparison.

Only then enlarge the model: add a club link, shaft compliance, declared contact
points, and body-side degrees of freedom as the question requires. Preserve
wrench points, projection axes, energy boundaries, and event definitions across
comparisons. Physical parameter changes need newly consistent states and
trajectories; relabeling coordinates does not create a new experiment.

The useful golf question is how body-side controls create a handle state and
club interaction while remaining responsive to loading. The hand path, club
reaction, shaft storage, and distal control are intertwined through the same
equations and energy boundaries. A moving-base model makes those assumptions
available for testing; it does not settle the golfer's best strategy by itself.
